controlsMoving.title: Controls: Moving Around
controlsMoving.description:
Arrows or WASD move. Z or Enter confirms and talks, X or Escape cancels. Hold Shift to run.

Running spends AP: a full meter is about ninety seconds. Walking refills it slowly, standing still quickly. Battle skills draw on the same meter.

Z acts on whatever you face. Z on a companion opens their Empathize sheet.

C kicks, always with the foot. Kicks break crates, force doors and shove objects. A kickable thing makes a sound; silence means it is not. Locked doors take seven to fifteen kicks.

controlsMenus.title: Controls: Menu Hotkeys
controlsMenus.description:
Tab opens the menu. Each screen also has a letter, pressed on the map:

- I inventory, C character, R equipment, P skills, J quests
- M minimap, B build, V vehicles, F factions, H holdings
- K cooking, L this book, N training, Y bestiary, U biologics
- O options, G sandbox (tester builds)

Inside the menu: 1 Thinker, 2 multiplayer, 3 Hypernet. On the map, 1 to 9 fire the quick bar.

WASD, Z, X, Q, E and T are reserved. F9 quicksave, F10 quickload, F11 fullscreen.

controlsMouse.title: Controls: Mouse
controlsMouse.description:
The mouse does not move your character.

- drag pans the camera, it snaps back when you walk
- wheel zooms, world map only
- hover shows an event's label, Alt labels them all

In battle: left click an enemy to hit it with the selected command, right click cycles commands, wheel scrolls, 1 to 5 fire.

Menus are clickable throughout.

controlsGamepad.title: Controls: Controller
controlsGamepad.description:
A controller works everywhere, menus, star map and 3D minigames included.

- left stick moves and navigates, right stick pans
- R3 labels every event on screen
- L2 / R2 zoom the world map, the right stick scrolls long overlays
- L1 / R1 cycle tabs, change character, step the quick bar

One thing still needs a mouse: opening a search field.

controlsRemap.title: Controls: Remapping
controlsRemap.description:
Options, Commands page. Keyboard and gamepad remap separately, and every default command can be rebound.

The ones added here: Zoom In (Q, LB), Zoom Out (E, RB), Kick (C, RT), Run (Shift, LT).

Bindings are kept with your settings.

controlsScreen.title: What Is On The Screen
controlsScreen.description:
The party HUD sits top left, on the map and in battle: name, level, HP, AP orb, MP. The acting member is lit.

Chips run beside each card. Hunger, sleep, hygiene, cravings and illness on the map; stat changes, class resources and states in battle. They colour past the warning line and again past the critical one.

While riding, the vehicle takes a row above the crew, fuel where magic would be.

The quick bar sits bottom centre: items on the map, skills in battle.

Notifications are parchment cards. Transient ones fade; standing ones stay while they are true.

The HUD can be switched off in Options, Video.

controlsSearch.title: Searching Inside Menus
controlsSearch.description:
Every long list carries the same search strip, this book included. It starts as a magnifier at the top of the page.

- while typing, no menu hotkey fires
- Escape empties the field, Escape again leaves it

The main menu search covers several screens at once: carried items, gear worn by companions, skills, recipes you can make now, bestiary creatures.

savingGame.title: Saving, Autosave and Quicksaves
savingGame.description:
The game autosaves on map change, at most once every few minutes, into an ordinary slot.

F9 quicksaves, F10 quickloads, over three rotating slots that any playthrough may overwrite.

Deleting a permadeath save leaves its diary behind.

worldsFolders.title: Worlds and Savegames
worldsFolders.description:
A world is a folder, and several can sit side by side. Make them from the Worlds screen. Until one exists, Explore, Reconnect, Story Mode and Sandbox stay greyed out.

A world is generated in full before it is played: a century of history, people, homes, jobs, shop rotas, the dungeon, politics, factions, epidemics.

Every playthrough in that world walks into the same place, already changed by the ones before it. The clock only moves forward, so a loaded save resumes from the latest date reached there.

Other playthroughs appear in person, standing where they were last saved.

optionsMenu.title: Options
optionsMenu.description:
Options is split into tabs, and plugins add rows rather than menus of their own.

- Video: resolution, fullscreen, pixel perfect scaling, retro shader, UI scaling, party HUD
- Audio: volumes, battle music picker
- Gameplay: party formation, auto idle explorer, world map hints
- Commands: keyboard and gamepad remapping
- Experimental: includes the local language model that can write NPC dialogue instead of the Markov chains

Fullscreen turns itself on the first time a distributed build runs, then keeps your setting.

modsUpdates.title: Mods and Updates
modsUpdates.description:
The game reads a mods folder next to the executable. Each subfolder mirrors the game's own folders, so a mod can replace a data file, add a picture or add content. Desktop build only.

In the Mod Manager, Enter toggles a mod and arrows move it in the load order. The bottom of the list wins.

The title screen has an Updates entry, which compares your files against the build's and downloads only what differs. Nothing is moved into place until everything is downloaded and checked, replaced files are backed up, and the game must be reopened. Two channels, stable and unstable, and any earlier build can be restored.

partyBasics.title: The Party
partyBasics.description:
Three members. The first is the leader: the one you steer, the one whose needs drain fastest, the one NPCs answer to.

A fourth companion walks along without being a member. It never fights and cannot be hurt.

Everyone keeps their own needs, opinions, reputation, specializations and standing with the other two.

Formation is set in Options. Close walks everyone in the leader's footsteps; Loose lets them wander and regroup off screen. A loose party acts on its own, and any meter under 35% sends that member off to eat, wash, play or rent a room out of the party purse.

Run for two seconds to call everyone in. Face a companion and confirm to open their Empathize sheet.

partyCreation.title: Making Your Characters
partyCreation.description:
Characters are made one at a time, three ways:

- Quick: look, class, traits, gear
- Dossiers: pre-made characters, some reusable in any world, the rest spent once used. A dossier may bring a vehicle, a hometown and alternate skins
- Detailed: the whole sheet, down to ideology, morality, orientation and backstory

Starting gear is picked by price, not power: the cheapest weapon of each type, on a fixed budget per class. Trait gear is granted on top.

partyClasses.title: Classes
partyClasses.description:
A class sets starting stats, the schools you learn fastest and a favoured element.

Each names a primary and a secondary category. Primary gives 3x progression at half price, secondary 1.5x at full price. Anything else needs a skill already known in that school and costs triple.

Training lists your curriculum only, though outside skills are still learnable.

Any class can equip any weapon; weapon skill is a trainable proficiency instead.

Creature classes are a separate set: Feral, Mimic, Monster, Mana Cyborg, Ghost, Zombie, Mutant, Drone. A character on one of them is an animal, not a person.

partyTraits.title: Traits
partyTraits.description:
Traits are bought at creation from a pool of points. Positive traits cost, negative traits pay back, so drawbacks fund virtues.

They change base stats and grant skills, items and gear, and they are read during play: NPC first impressions, how much anyone minds your condition, which specializations start ahead, what companions do with their free time.

Traits are permanent.

partyAttributes.title: Attributes
partyAttributes.description:
Six attributes:

- STR: carrying capacity, physical damage
- CON: damage absorbed, how long a choke is held
- DEX: speed, precision, evasion, escaping holds
- INT: learning, mathematical magic
- WIS: judgement, resistance, intuitive magic
- PSI: luck. Enemy reactions, loot rolls, hidden rolls in your favour

The battle HUD shows the modifier as a multiplier (STR 1.4x).

partyCreatures.title: Playing A Creature
partyCreatures.description:
A party member can be a creature, built from one archetype or two crossed.

The archetype drives the body: the limb and organ system gives it exactly that species' parts, reach, hands and weak points.

A creature class is non sentient, with no conversation, politics, savings or property. A civilised class is a person shaped like an animal, treated as a person everywhere.

Anatomy is mechanical, not cosmetic. It decides how many weapons can be held, whether you can be choked, and what a pregnancy produces.

partyPortraits.title: Portraits and 3D Models
partyPortraits.description:
Each character is drawn one of three ways, chosen at creation and never mixed:

- bust: hand drawn portrait
- model: procedural 3D body. Each limb can take the matching part of any registered creature, with sliders for height, build, ears, nose and skin
- sprite: used by monsters, recruited enemies and summons, shown as the 3D model of their species

The status screen, the dialogue busts and the Empathize panel all use it.

partyRecruiting.title: Recruiting People
partyRecruiting.description:
Three ways into the party: talk a monster round in battle, ask a townsperson through Empathize once they think well enough of whoever is asking, or adopt a creature and train it up.

A recruited townsperson leaves the map for good. Their profile, personality, traits, skills, wealth, history and standing all move into the party actor.

The party holds three, so someone must leave for someone to join. Retired members go back to the dossier board.

partyPets.title: Pets, Followers and Children
partyPets.description:
A fourth companion follows the party without being a member. It never fights, cannot die and cannot be targeted.

A follower is a creature recruited from a monster that talks, a pet one from a monster that does not, a child the result of a pregnancy.

Only one walks with you at a time; the Followers page swaps and releases them.

Pets and followers can be trained into party members, at classes the species roster allows. Training is measured in world clock minutes, Animal Training or Leadership shortens it, and only the companion currently walking with you makes progress. Children and summons are never trained.

partyReproduction.title: Reproduction and Pregnancy
partyReproduction.description:
Every body has a reproductive type, set at creation from the species:

- Testicles: fertility, count, motility and morphology answer to hormones and condition
- Uterus: a 28 day cycle, fertile on days 12 to 16
- Oviparous: a clutch of one to four eggs
- Plant: seeds develop endlessly and stockpile until planted
- Mitosis: the body divides and makes a copy

A pregnancy runs the term of the species. Biologics shows gestational age and fetal stage, symptoms arrive as states, and the heart rate climbs.

Newborns register in Followers as children with the parent's face. Mitosis makes a copy, not a child.

partyDeath.title: Death, Gravestones and Permadeath
partyDeath.description:
Falling in battle is not automatic death. Health protection and danger warnings let you break off, and fleeing always works.

A dead character leaves a gravestone where they fell. It stays on the map and is where restoration is performed.

Under permadeath the character is gone for good and their quicksaves with them. A wiped party ends that party only; the next starts in the same changed world.

Lost limbs are not death and healing does not put them back.

partyBanterPage.title: What Your Companions Say
partyBanterPage.description:
Two or more companions hold discussions of two to four lines, drawn from whatever is happening: a recent purchase, low health, a meter under 35%, a diary line from the last few hours, the biome, the road, the money, the leader, the plan.

A third member's personality usually closes the exchange, so the same script reads differently depending on who is there. The same purchase draws a resentful line from the disciplined member, a why only one from the hedonist.

They talk while driving too, and on trains, coaches and taxis. A party of one talks to itself.

partyAutoIdle.title: The Auto Explorer
partyAutoIdle.description: An Options toggle lets the game play itself while you are idle. The party explores, crosses the map and looks after its needs the way a loose companion does, paying the same costs you would, and hands control back the moment you press anything.

progressLevels.title: Levels and Experience
progressLevels.description:
Experience comes from winning fights, and a level raises the six attributes and the HP and MP pools.

Levels are a small part of power. Skills learned, specializations trained, gear carried and the condition of the body all matter more.

progressKnowledge.title: Knowledge Points
progressKnowledge.description:
Knowledge points buy skills, and KP belongs to the party rather than to one member. They come from fights scaled against the party's median level, from quests, adventures, dreams and Raman scans.

Prices are computed from combat value: MP and AP cost, damage scaling, repeats, targets hit, states inflicted. The weakest skill is 50 KP, an ordinary one a few hundred, the strongest a couple of thousand. Esoteric costs ten times its score, Forbidden a hundred times.

Primary school halves the price, secondary pays full, outside schools triple it.

progressAtlas.title: The Atlas of Circles
progressAtlas.description:
Skills are laid out as a sphere grid. Each school is an alchemical circle: rings from its weakest working outward to its strongest, joined by spokes, with upgrade spurs on the rim ending in esoteric workings.

You can only buy a skill adjacent to one you know, and one known neighbour is enough. The innermost ring of every school is always open.

Forbidden workings sit alone in the centre, connected to nothing. The whole school must be known before any opens.

One school at a time: use the pager or walk off the rim. Wheel and Shift zoom, drag pans.

progressTraining.title: Training and Progression
progressTraining.description: Each member trains one skill at a time. Winning a battle is worth 3 points, using a skill of the same category 2. Primary categories multiply this by 3, secondary by 1.5.

progressSpecializations.title: Specializations
progressSpecializations.description:
About eight hundred specializations, from Wrestling to Accounting to Beekeeping. Each is governed by one attribute and has five tiers, Untrained to Master.

A level is the highest of three sources: trained through play, granted by class, granted by a trait.

They train by doing. Cooking raises cooking, selling raises haggling. The leader earns full value, anyone else present 35%.

They are read everywhere: forging quality, lockpicking, hold damage, what a merchant accepts, whether a recipe can be read at all.

progressPassives.title: Class Passives
progressPassives.description:
Every class has signature passives. They need no slot and no activation. Some work in combat, some only outside it.

They are listed on the status sheet under Passives.

progressLoadout.title: The Nine Skill Slots
progressLoadout.description:
A character carries nine skills into a fight, out of everything they know. The skill menu is tabbed by role, and the nine chosen fill the battle quick bar.

Everything known stays known, and changing the loadout between fights is free.

progressFusion.title: Fusing Spells
progressFusion.description:
From the Magic page, two abilities can be forged into one. The dominant slot takes a spell you know and sets damage, scope, hit type and icon. The recessive slot takes a spell or a skill, and a skill makes the result a skill.

The fusion costs the sum of its parts in MP and AP, and the sum of their teaching prices in KP. The components are forgotten on fusing, and the fusion can be split back into them at any time.

progressGrimoires.title: Grimoires and Skill Books
progressGrimoires.description:
A grimoire offers five random workings and lets one reader claim one. The five are rolled once when the book is opened, against the whole party; switching reader does not reroll them.

A reader can only claim an offer whose MP cost fits their maximum MP and that they do not already know. The party's median PSI raises the chance of a Forbidden working turning up.

There are school specific grimoires, category specific skill books, and the Forbidden Grimoire, which offers nothing else.

progressBladeSeeds.title: Blade Seeds
progressBladeSeeds.description:
Twelve seeds, one per weapon type. A seed is a permanent upgrade path for a whole weapon type rather than for one weapon.

It grows as that type is used, and what it grows into is procedural, so no two worlds grow the same blade. A seed outlasts the weapon that carried it.

gearSlots.title: Equipment: Hands and Slots
gearSlots.description:
There is no dual wield flag. Weapon slots come from anatomy: every body part the species can hold a weapon with is a slot. Hands take a weapon or a shield without distinction, so two shields are as legal as two swords.

- a two handed weapon needs two free hands
- a body with no hands holds its weapon in the mouth, and anything fits. Samurai keep a mouth slot on top of their hands
- eight slots maximum, however many limbs a body has
- past two weapons each parameter becomes the median of what is carried, and two random weapons swing each turn
- losing a limb removes its slot and drops what it held

gearProficiency.title: Weapon Proficiency
gearProficiency.description:
Any class can equip any weapon type. Skill with a weapon is a specialization, one per type, twelve in all, starting at Intermediate for the types your class was once limited to and Untrained for the rest.

It scales the weapon's parameters: 33% Untrained, 67% Beginner, 100% Intermediate, 110% Advanced, 125% Master.

Winning a battle grants one point per equipped weapon type.

gearScaling.title: What a Weapon Scales On
gearScaling.description: A weapon does not always scale on STR. Its attack skill sets the attribute it reads, and the equip screen names it when the slot is selected. With no attack skill it reads STR; otherwise DEX, INT, WIS, CON, PSI, or a mix of two.

gearArmor.title: Armour and Derived Stats
gearArmor.description:
Equipment feeds four out of combat stats besides defence. Clothes give Substance and Stealth, robes Arcane, light armour Stealth, heavy armour Intimidation.

Weapons feed them too: daggers and bows Stealth, swords, heavy weapons, axes and claws Intimidation, staves Arcane, whips, projectiles and guns Substance.

They decide how people answer you, what a guard assumes, which approaches are open.

gearModifiers.title: Modifiers on Gear
gearModifiers.description:
A weapon or armour piece can carry one modifier, which changes its stats, price and traits. Sharp raises STR and price on weapons, Refined raises CON, WIS and price on anything, Poisoned adds poison to a weapon, Worn lowers CON, WIS and price on armour.

The modifier is part of the item and moves with it.

gearWeight.title: Weight and Encumbrance
gearWeight.description: Every item has a weight and the party has a carry capacity. Going over it raises a standing notification that stays up until you are back under.

gearBackpack.title: The Backpack
gearBackpack.description:
The backpack is tabbed by category, with the weight readout, the detail card and the favourites bar.

Nine favourite slots hold usable items and share the quick bar with battle skills. On the map, 1 to 9 use that slot; in the backpack, the same keys assign the inspected item. Items can be dragged onto slots, right click clears one.

Only usable items can be favourited. Weapons and armour are equipped instead.

gearArtifacts.title: Artifacts
gearArtifacts.description:
Artifacts are procedurally generated items, weapons and armour, each named and unique.

The Artifact Analyzer on the Hypernet reads what an unfamiliar one does.

gearContainers.title: Containers and Storage
gearContainers.description:
Chests, cupboards, crates and sacks store items and can be emptied or filled at will.

The party's own storage travels with it: the extradimensional container, and the holds of the camper and the car.

gearRarity.title: Loot and Rarity
gearRarity.description:
Random loot is scaled against the party's median level, not the leader's.

Items print in their rarity colour everywhere: reward popup, backpack, shop counter.

Item descriptions are combinatorial and resolved from the world seed, so the same sword reads the same way all through one world and differently in the next.

needsOverview.title: The Five Needs
needsOverview.description:
Everyone in the world, your party included, carries five meters: Hunger, Sleep, Hygiene, Company and Fun.

All five run 100 to 0 and drain with time, and time passes as you walk: a minute per ten steps, ten minutes per world map tile, two in a vehicle. The leader drains fastest and running drains everything faster.

They show as chips beside each party card, colouring below 20% and again at 0. Every change is announced with the party median.

At 0, hunger drains HP, sleep drains MP, and the rest cost you socially and mentally.

Augments can slow a need, stop it or reverse it: a ruminant stomach burns less, a somnologic regulator never tires, a self cleaning dermis gains hygiene as you walk.

needsHunger.title: Hunger and Nutrition
needsHunger.description:
Every edible item carries calories, fat and protein, and eating credits all three. What a meal is worth comes from its contents, not its price.

Hunger can pass 100, up to 150%. Above 110% you are overfed, which is a state with penalties, and above 100 it burns three times faster.

Temperature costs food at both ends: cold burns calories for warmth, heat raises metabolism.

At 0 you take continuous HP damage until you eat.

needsSleep.title: Sleep, Rest and Time Awake
needsSleep.description:
Two separate values are tracked.

The sleep meter is how tired you feel. Coffee or a sit down refills it, and at 0 it drains MP.

Time since you last slept is a stamp on the world clock that only a night's rest clears: zero up to a day awake, climbing through two, maxed at a week. It is what turns dreams hostile and pulls the party's mind apart.

Beds, campfires, tents and world map camps open the rest menu, and sleep refills the meter whatever hour you wake at. Wait and the T hotkey only move the clock. Cryogenic sleep is separate: pick a year to wake in and the world moves on without you.

needsHygiene.title: Hygiene, and What It Costs You
needsHygiene.description:
Hygiene drains slightly faster than sleep. Refill it at a washroom, shower, sink or fountain; loose companions go and find one below 35%.

It works both ways: your hygiene is read against the person you talk to, and theirs against you. At 60% and above nobody notices; below that each point costs a little under half a point of standing, capped at 45.

Traits set how much it matters. Feral ignores it, Ascetic barely notices, Street Urchin, Cave Dweller, Survivalist, Farmer and Veteran mind little. Proud, Wealthy, Beautiful, Perfectionist, Noble, Hypochondriac and Germaphobe mind a lot. Several such traits multiply; one "does not notice" trait overrides them all.

Courting reads both bodies again at a heavier weight, and names which of the two needs a bath.

needsSocial.title: Company
needsSocial.description:
Company drains like any other need and is refilled by talking, to townspeople or between two of your own.

A loose member starved of company walks up to someone and starts a conversation unprompted. That conversation moves what the other person thinks of them, and hygiene counts in it.

Gaining standing with someone feeds the social meter of whoever gained it.

needsLeisure.title: Fun
needsLeisure.description:
Fun is refilled by playing: arcade cabinets, pianos, pool tables, card games, and jokes that land in conversation. A joke that lands also raises the listener's Fun for the rest of the day.

A party with Fun on the floor complains about it in banter.

needsAddiction.title: Cravings and Withdrawal
needsAddiction.description:
Five traits are dependencies: alcohol, caffeine, nicotine, narcotics and gambling. Only a member with one has a craving meter.

A craving runs backwards. It climbs while unfed, 0 is satisfied, 100 is withdrawal, and feeding it drops it to 0. Withdrawal starts at a full meter and only lifts once the craving is well below it, so one dose does not clear it.

Cravings climb slower during sleep, and always on the member carrying the trait.

bodyParts.title: Limbs and Organs
bodyParts.description:
Every character and monster has individual limbs and organs, each with its own health, taken from its species.

Damage spreads across parts. A part at 0 is destroyed, carries a permanent penalty while it stays that way, and changes what the body can do: a lost hand takes its weapon slot, a body with no hands holds a weapon in its mouth, damaged legs cost movement and evasion. A part at 0, damaged or severed can neither grapple nor be grappled.

Vital organs are shielded from ordinary damage and only opened by deliberate targeting.

Parts never heal on their own. They are treated at a clinic, restored by magic, or replaced with a prosthetic. In Blood and Oil a slashing blow can take a part off the body, carrying its augment with it.

The status sheet has an Anatomy section showing the body part by part.

bodyBiologics.title: Biologics
bodyBiologics.description:
Biologics is the deep readout: vital signs, hormones, blood chemistry, brain regions and their activity, blood type, reproductive cycle, and every condition acting on the body.

Heart rate answers to what is happening to you, hormones to sleep, injury and pregnancy. Blood type is set once and never changes.

The Ley Vein system links it to limb damage: blockages show up here when the body has been hurt.

healthDiseases.title: Diseases
healthDiseases.description:
Hundreds of diseases exist. Each has a transmission chance, one or more vectors (airborne, saliva, bite, contact, sexual and others), stat modifiers while carried, and often a state that only appears after the carrier has walked a set number of steps. That delay is the window period.

Transmission is rolled between your own members each time you open the pause menu, and between the party and a townsperson each time you open their Empathize panel. Venereal diseases never spread by proximity.

Every NPC carries a medical history seeded from the world, readable on the Health tab of their panel.

Diagnose examines the whole party and names every illness carried, window period included.

healthEpidemics.title: Epidemics
healthEpidemics.description:
A continental epidemic model runs above individual illness, whether or not you are watching it. Each infected town runs its own curve, resolved at midnight, and exports cases along map distance with occasional long jumps. Public response builds the longer a town has been infected, and eventually breaks the wave.

A medical outbreak is a pathogen with a case fatality ratio. A hysteria has none: dancing fever, genital theft panics, phantom gassers. A hysteria is caught by witnessing it and spread by talking about it.

Every world starts with three running: one hysteria, one ordinary outbreak, one rare and mortal.

Anyone in an infected town is exposed, you included. Outbreaks move mood, hiring, shop traffic, need drain, gossip and the news, and the Eurodemics observatory tracks all of it.

healthSurgery.title: Clinics, Prosthetics and Field Surgery
healthSurgery.description:
A clinic can install a body part, remove one, replace one or fit an implant. Installing costs 1000 euros per percent of body health the part represents, removal 100, and vital parts cannot be removed.

Field surgery is the same operation on the road: pick a patient and a surgeon, fit only parts already carried, take an augment out but never seat one, and pay nothing.

Every operation is a roll, with the odds shown first. The surgeon's Surgery specialization gives 35 / 50 / 65 / 78 / 90 percent by tier, then a roof is +10, a cave -5, the open -10, rain -15, a storm -25, snow +5, and operating on yourself -15.

A failure wounds the patient elsewhere. Vital organs are only at risk in Blood and Oil.

healthAugments.title: Augments
healthAugments.description:
The Augments register has two lists. Fitted is every augment the party wears, with its wearer and socket. Catalogue is everything that exists, readable before paying to have it grafted.

The dossier gives the cost, the bonus, the skill it teaches, and every socket that accepts it, creature sockets included.

Augments are also how the needs system is bent: the right hardware slows a meter, stops it, or reverses it.

healthWeatherBody.title: Weather, Temperature and the Body
healthWeatherBody.description:
Ambient temperature is a number, shown on the travel card, and it acts on the body. Cold burns calories for warmth and heat raises metabolism, so hunger drains faster at both ends.

Weather also costs field surgery: rain -15, storms -25, snow +5. And it drives what people do and where they are.

combatBasics.title: How a Fight Starts
combatBasics.description:
There are no random encounters. Every monster stands on the map with its level over its head, and you fight it by walking into it.

Turns are individual: each battler acts when its own turn comes up, in agility order, and your action resolves the moment you choose it.

Enemies keep their damage between fights. A wounded monster you ran from is still wounded when you come back, and corpses stay on the map.

Fleeing always works.

combatCommands.title: The Battle Commands
combatCommands.description:
The command menu holds Attack, Guard, Skills, Magic, Item, Escape, Reload when a firearm is empty, and four of its own:

- Check: opens the enemy's body, limb by limb, with the chance of hitting each
- Target: aims your next blow at one part
- Wrestle: takes hold of the enemy
- Talk: another way to end a fight

Wrestle and Talk are commands, not skills. They take no loadout slot, cannot be forgotten, and come from the body rather than the class.

Mouse: left click an enemy to run the selected command on it, right click cycles, wheel scrolls, 1 to 5 fire.

combatAP.title: MP and AP
combatAP.description:
Two resources. MP is magic: spells cost it, it refills slowly, and most rites and summons are held with it.

AP is momentum, capped at 100, spent by battle skills and by sprinting on the map out of the same meter. Running empties it in about ninety seconds, walking refills it slowly, standing still fast.

Cost follows type: magic is written in CamelCase and costs MP, a skill is written in plain words and costs AP.

combatBodyParts.title: Hitting What You Aim At
combatBodyParts.description:
Monsters have the same limbs and organs the party does. Check lists every part with its condition and the chance to hit it, and Target aims your next blow at one. The chance comes from the part's size, your weapon type read against your stats, and a random swing of ten percent either way.

Destroying a limb removes what it does: a broken leg slows, a ruined wing stops flight, no hands means no weapon held. Vital organs can only be reached by a targeted attack.

Part damage persists through the fight, and a finishing blow can sever the part.

combatDamageTypes.title: Damage Types & Piercing Mechanics
combatDamageTypes.description:
Every attack, skill and weapon carries a damage type: Explosive, Piercing, Cutting, Blunt, Area, Abstract or None.

Explosive, Piercing and Cutting can sever a part on a lethal blow; the rest ruin it in place. Area and Explosive spread over two to four parts, everything else puts all of it into the part aimed at.

Piercing also ignores most defences. It punches through Guard for half damage, hits a Protect substitute in full and carries through to the ally behind for half, ignores Divine Shield completely, and passes through Magic Reflection to hit the target directly.

combatWrestle.title: Wrestling
combatWrestle.description:
Wrestle is open to any body with one limb whole enough to grip. It costs nothing and is never learned.

It replaces the command menu with the grapple plan: which of your limbs takes the hold, which of theirs it is taken on, and which hold. Each row shows the odds. A part at 0, damaged or severed can neither grab nor be grabbed, on either side.

- Grapple, STR against DEX: takes hold. Everything else needs one first
- Strike, STR against DEX: needs no hold, can concuss on the head
- Joint lock, DEX against STR: pins, often breaks the guard
- Wrench, STR against CON: heavy damage, can cause bleeding
- Slam, CON against DEX: guard broken, winded, chance to stun
- Choke, CON against CON, head only: guard broken, vitals exposed
- Rip, STR against CON: low odds, enormous damage, can tear the limb off

Everything scales with the Wrestling specialization. Any trained martial art adds its own finishers without them being learned as skills.

combatTalk.title: Talking to Monsters
combatTalk.description:
A monster tagged as able to understand you can be talked to. Talk opens a panel with the odds of each approach printed beside it.

Every enemy carries a disposition from 1 to 100, rolled when it appears and shifted by species, and hurting it costs 5 to 15 points.

- Chat builds rapport. Chance is disposition plus a fifth of the gap between your PSI and its own, floor 10%, cap 95%
- Surrender, same odds. It leaves the fight
- Join the party needs a free slot, and above 80 disposition it uses the chat chance
- Follow you, or be adopted as a pet. A talker needs 70 disposition
- Insult always lands and lowers disposition
- Throw a stone, or pet it

Creatures marked as forces rather than people, petrodemons above all, refuse every approach.

One talked into joining becomes a party member. One taken as pet or follower can be trained into a member later.

combatEnemyLevels.title: Enemy Levels and Where They Live
combatEnemyLevels.description:
The Enemy Spawn option sets how enemy levels are chosen.

Balanced draws from a band above the party's median: median L meets L to L + 7 + L/10. One encounter per world tile sits above the band as a boss, never over 100.

Distance from spawn, the default, sets level by how far the world square lies from the one you started on: level 1 at home, the top of the roster at the far corner. Each square fields creatures whose habitat matches the biome.

Chaos deals the whole roster flat random, 1 to 110, redealt on every map entry.

No creature is exclusive to a country. Every nation holds every creature its biomes hold, and only changes how common each is.

The calendar sits above all three. In 2001 the band is as the mode sets it; from 2002 to 2009 it climbs ten levels a year; 2010 and 2011 have no band at all; from 2012 nothing below level 80 roams, and there is no ceiling.

combatMovementAI.title: How Monsters Behave
combatMovementAI.description:
Each roaming monster carries a movement personality that sets what it does while idle, how it notices you (sight range, facing cone, line of sight) and what it does once it has.

Fixed, Random, Approach, Fleeing, Skittish, Grazer, Sentry, Guard, Patrol, Territorial, Ambusher, Lurker, Mimic, Swooper, Stalker, Hunter, Charger, Pack, Erratic, Drifter, Orbiter, Scavenger, Coward.

A Grazer never notices you. A Sentry has a cone and can be walked around. An Ambusher is not where it appears to be. A Pack does not fight alone.

combatSafety.title: Danger Warnings and Surviving a Blow
combatSafety.description:
Before a fight the party's median level is compared with the enemy, and a warning appears when it is out of range. Enemy levels are drawn over their heads on the map.

Inside a fight each character has one health protection charge: the first blow that would kill them leaves them at 1 HP. It comes back next battle. Blood and Oil removes it.

combatModes.title: Difficulty and Combat Modes
combatModes.description:
Several settings change what combat is, most chosen at character creation.

- Peaceful: monsters act only once hurt, per enemy. An unprovoked one skips its turn, roaming monsters wander instead of chasing, and a wipe respawns you with nobody dead
- Ordinary: death leaves a gravestone and the run continues
- Hardcore and Blood and Oil: death is a game over and the character is removed. Blood and Oil also drops the health protection charge and lets a slashing blow take a part off the body
- Card combat: replaces the command menu
- Map battle: fights on the live map

combatMapBattle.title: Map Battle Mode
combatMapBattle.description:
An experimental option fights every battle on the map you are standing on instead of a battle screen.

Everyone fights from where they stand; only a member off screen is placed. Every other monster keeps its position and behaviour, and any that wanders within a few tiles joins in with its own HP card and turn slot. A townsperson near the brawl joins your side if the party is well liked or if they are brave, fighting from their own level, stats and skills.

Move repositions the acting battler at a range driven by agility. Weapons have reach: 1 melee, 2 for spears, whips, staves and flails, more for bows, guns and thrown weapons, line of sight required. Stepping into water means swimming, which costs more movement.

Round order: party and enemies interleaved by agility, then townspeople, then the world step, where every roaming monster, townsperson and your pet take one tile at once.

combatSummons.title: Summons
combatSummons.description:
A summon is a temporary fourth member. In battle it lives for that battle only: never saved, never in the menu, gone when the fight ends or when you stop paying for it.

What answers: a creature, a person the party has marked, the pet on your leash, a reflection of the summoner, or a revenant of a traveller you lost.

Numbers are re-cut against your median and the troop on the field, then multiplied by the rite's share: a familiar is half a traveller, a titan slightly more than one. Shape is kept, so a bruiser stays a bruiser. The petrodemon is held by your oil, and the elder entity arrives with its own numbers and drains the summoner in about three turns.

Upkeep by kind: HP for demons, undead, shadows, swarms and titans; MP for elementals, celestials, fae and the void; AP for the reflection; euros for constructs, war machines, dragons and champions; soul for spirits; oil for the petrodemon; a fixed few turns for beasts, verdants, familiars and called people. When you cannot pay, it leaves, and a summoner who cannot pay in blood is left at 1 HP.

The familiar belongs to one character. Their class decides which creature answers and its name is rolled once from theirs, so changing class remakes the pact.

While a summon is out, a hyper bar fills with damage the party deals. Full, the summon fires its ultimate, which grows with the party's median level in brackets of ten.

A summon is always computer controlled and has no 1 HP protection.

Outside a fight the same rites work and what they call walks in a trailing slot, each point of MP buying a fixed number of steps.

combatArena.title: The Arena
combatArena.description:
The arena fights for its own sake, in two shapes: a gauntlet, a run of fights in a chosen level bracket, and a biome trial, a run against the fauna of a chosen biome.

The party is rescaled to the bracket, and a random roster can be fielded instead of your own.

Wins build a streak, which pays ascending money and items.

combatBulletHell.title: Bullet Hell Sequences
combatBulletHell.description:
Some fights break into a bullet hell sequence: you steer a small craft, dodge the enemy's pattern and shoot back.

Damage taken and dealt there counts in the fight.

combatSpirits.title: Spirit Battlers
combatSpirits.description:
Defeated enemies join a spirit roster. One can be fielded in place of an ordinary battler, at a cost that scales with what it was.

The feature runs on its own switch, and a world with it off fights ordinary battles.

combatMimic.title: Mimicry
combatMimic.description:
Six mimic skills copy other bodies:

- Partial mimicry: the enemy's face and map sprite, numbers unchanged
- Full mimicry: stats, HP, MP, AP, skills, body and looks
- Mirror: re-executes the enemy's last skill against it
- Copy ally: a companion's name, class, skills, sprite and body
- Random: full mimicry of a creature drawn at random
- Mutation: merges two random archetypes into your own body parts

All six need exactly one enemy on the field. Copying a body copies its limbs, which changes what you can hold and where you can be hurt.

combatThrow.title: Throwing Things
combatThrow.description:
Items, weapons and armour can be thrown up to eight tiles, diagonals included, with flight simulated from the item's weight. Heavy things travel a short way and land hard.

A thrown item stays where it lands and anyone can pick it up.

combatCorpses.title: Corpses, Rewards and Cooldowns
combatCorpses.description:
After a fight the reward popup names everything at once: items in their rarity colours, money, experience and knowledge, the last scaled by enemy level against the party median.

The dead leave corpses on the map, and enemy events are removed or put behind a cooldown rather than respawning at once.

Every creature met is written into the Bestiary.

elementsOverview.title: Elements: How They Work
elementsOverview.description:
Nine damage types: Physical, Fire, Ice, Thunder, Water, Petro, Wind, Sacred, Cursed.

Every creature answers each with a rate. Above 100% is a weakness, below is resistance, 0% is immunity, and a negative rate absorbs the element and heals from it.

The battle HUD prints what you have discovered about the enemy in front of you, and the Bestiary keeps it.

States interact: Wet raises lightning damage, Oily raises fire damage, Static absorbs lightning. A class leans toward an element, and a weapon or modifier can carry one.

elementPhysical.title: Element: Physical
elementPhysical.description:
Edges, points, weight and fists. Most weapons deal it and most armour is built to stop it.

Physical damage severs limbs, breaks guards and lands holds. Heavy armour resists it and feeds Intimidation, light armour trades that for Stealth.

Spirits, oozes and gases resist it.

elementFire.title: Element: Fire
elementFire.description:
Applies Burned, which keeps dealing damage after the blow.

Raised against anything oily, dry or wooden. Resisted by the wet and the cold blooded, absorbed by things that live in fire.

elementIce.title: Element: Ice
elementIce.description:
Applies Cold, and Freeze at strength, which stops a body acting.

Raised against wet targets. Used on a burning target it removes the burn.

elementThunder.title: Element: Thunder
elementThunder.description:
Applies Static, and Paralysis at strength.

Devastating against a wet target. Absorbed by anything already Static, which heals it instead.

Machines and constructs usually resist it.

elementWater.title: Element: Water
elementWater.description:
Applies Wet, which raises lightning damage, lowers fire damage and is read by several states.

Its own damage is low.

petro.title: Element: Petro
petro.description:
Oil and what comes out of the ground with it.

Petro belongs to the petrodemons, which cannot be talked to, petted or reasoned with, and which drop barrels rather than coins. Oil works as a currency: it prices the post between worlds, it holds the petrodemon summon on the field, and the market trades it.

Petro damage leaves the target flammable.

elementWind.title: Element: Wind
elementWind.description:
Air, pressure and cutting motion. It unbalances and displaces.

Flying creatures deal it and resist it. It is weakest against rooted or heavy targets.

elementSacred.title: Element: Sacred
elementSacred.description:
Answered badly by the undead and the cursed. It is the one damage type that heals its target when that target is on the right side of the line.

Sacred workings usually carry protection and purging alongside damage, and several sit deep in expensive schools.

elementCursed.title: Element: Cursed
elementCursed.description:
Rot, ruin and draining. Dealt by the undead, answered by the sacred.

Cursed workings often cost more than MP, and the strongest are tagged Forbidden, which puts them alone at the centre of their circle at a hundred times their value.

Efficient against the living. It heals the already dead.

worldMapPage.title: The World Map
worldMapPage.description:
The world map is one map of Europe, each tile a whole region. Walking one costs ten minutes of game time, two in a vehicle.

M cycles the display: hidden, corner minimap, fullscreen. In fullscreen, drag to pan, wheel or Q and E to zoom.

Stepping onto a tile offers to keep going or to visit the square, which builds its local map. T switches between the world map and the last local map.

Loose companions keep a two tile leash up there, and squares marked "???" are adventures.

worldProcedural.title: Procedural Maps
worldProcedural.description:
Almost every map is generated. A world map square becomes a map when you enter it, built from the world seed and its coordinates, so it is the same map every time you return.

The biome sets the tileset and what grows there. Roads run straight, cross, turn and loop back at the middle of the map when they lead nowhere. Rivers are wide and irregular, snapping to a fixed width at the borders so they continue into the next square, and only reach a border if the square beyond is water. Coastlines are sampled along the border line so neighbours draw one continuous shore. On top of that go hand authored 32x32 prefabs and terrain features scattered by biome.

Walking off the edge loads the neighbouring square directly.

worldBiomes.title: Biomes
worldBiomes.description:
The biome of a square sets its tileset, terrain features, fauna, music, weather and forageables.

Some are special variants, rolled rather than fixed: spirit woods, crystal fields. Certain creatures live only there, and a special biome always places at least one of them, whatever the spawn mode or the calendar.

Roofed biomes, cellars, temple interiors, cave dens and dungeons, are entered through a structure entrance instead of walked into.

worldStructures.title: Structures Under the Map
worldStructures.description:
Entrances on procedural maps are walked into, not pressed. What lies behind is rolled from the world seed, the square and the tile, so one stairway always leads to the same place.

- stairs down: any structure. Cellar, dungeon, crypt, catacombs, mine, cistern, warren, oubliette, library, forge, bunker, laboratory, shrine, tunnel, grotto, lava tube, barrow, station, salt works, cave den, temple
- stairs up: things built above ground and since buried
- cave: dens, frozen caves, crystal caves, fungal caves, lava tubes, sea grottoes
- grate: a sewer, only in towns that declare one underneath
- hatch: a patron's vault, full of money and rare weapons

The surface limits the options: ice fields hold frozen caves, a graveyard holds catacombs.

worldHouses.title: Houses, Inns and Shops
worldHouses.description:
Doors on procedural maps are handed to the building system. Pools of houses, inns, shops and tower blocks are seeded by coordinates, so a door is always the same business.

Buildings can have several floors and are configured as data. Shops and inns wear their name over the door.

Doors open with an animation when walked into, and the lock is checked before it runs.

worldTerrain.title: Working the Terrain
worldTerrain.description:
Face a terrain feature and press the action button to work it. Trees are felled with an axe in the inventory, rocks mined with a war pick, any heavy weapon or a chipped pickaxe, plants picked with nothing at all, and anything can be dismantled.

The payout is crafting materials. Mining sometimes yields an ingot.

Foraging always pays plant matter, and about two picks in five also pay something edible. What turns up depends on the country: acorns and chanterelles in a forest, cloudberries on tundra, dates in a desert, samphire on a marsh, blind mushrooms underground. Training Foraging raises the odds. A feature that is a specific plant pays that plant anywhere.

Alien surfaces forage nothing. Their food comes from butchering local wildlife.

Felled trees and worked features stay gone when the map is rebuilt, scenery inside a prefab included.

worldDungeon.title: The Dungeon and the Tower
worldDungeon.description:
One great dungeon, its layout rolled when the world is created.

Above ground it runs in ten levels, A to J, each of nine ordinary floors and one elevator floor. The elevator and the floor list jump to any floor already reached; unseen floors show as question marks.

Below ground is the lower tower, ninety two generated floors, each one of the structures from the procedural catalogue. Stairs read the other way down there: deeper is a smaller number.

worldPuzzles.title: Puzzles
worldPuzzles.description:
Maps carry puzzles:

- sokoban blocks, pits that swallow them, goal tiles, reset and undo shrines
- pressure plates, timed plates that must be held, levers, gates wired with and / or logic
- ice floors, arrow tiles, conveyors
- crystal switches that flip sets of blocks between solid and open
- torches to light, sometimes timed, sometimes spreading fire
- colour tiles, lights out grids, coloured doors, combination locks
- warp pads, crackable walls, light beams to redirect, clones that copy your moves, magnetic objects, counterweights, floodable rooms

worldFog.title: Fog of War
worldFog.description:
Some maps are covered in fog, pushed back by walking. Vision is a cone, not a circle: you see where you face, and turning is how you look around.

Uncovered ground is remembered per map.

worldDigging.title: Digging and Secret Doors
worldDigging.description:
Some walls can be broken through at runtime, turning a dead end into a route. Digging is the deliberate version.

Secret doors look like wall until interacted with, then fade, make a noise and stay open.

Locked doors give three options. Peek teleports you for a look without letting you move, and the menu that follows holds the other two: pick, which plays a falling block minigame and needs lockpicks, or break in, which is filed as a crime.

worldMovement.title: Water, Climbing and Bridges
worldMovement.description:
Face water and press the action button to open the water menu: swim, which changes the sprite and disables sprinting, fish, with a rod in the party, or dive under the surface.

Climbable terrain is climbed slowly, facing up, with companions hidden. Height is tracked, and jumping down from three tiles or more costs 5% health per tile fallen.

Bridges are layered. Enter from the approach and you walk on the bridge; enter from anywhere else and you pass under it, and the layer holds across the whole span.

A mirror shows an upright reflection of whoever stands in front of it.

worldWeather.title: Weather, Time and Seasons
worldWeather.description:
The clock starts at 8 AM on 1 January 2001 and never stops. Time advances as you walk and jumps when you sleep, wait or travel.

Weather is generated per country, seeded on the date, and changes on entering an outdoor map. The country sets sunrise and sunset, seasonal temperatures, and which weather is possible.

Rain applies Wet, storms apply Static, snow applies Hot, from the body burning to stay warm.

The screen is tinted by time of day and by temperature, blue for cold and red for hot. Rain and night carry ambient sound on their own channel.

worldDreams.title: Dreams
worldDreams.description:
Sleeping can drop you into a dream: a full 3D world rolled from a seed. It deals four to seven regions and mixes them: backrooms, offices, escher stairs, drowned places, cosmic voids, megastructures, car parks, hospitals, cathedrals, factories, carnivals, sewers, fleshpits, gardens, ruins.

- WASD walks, the mouse looks, space jumps. Hold jump while standing still to take off
- the action button uses the weapon in your right hand; the wheel steps a shuffled rack of every weapon in the game
- touching anything alive moves you to another dream, and so does walking head on into a wall
- holes have no floor, and falling far enough leaves the dream

Every dream carries one to three laws: the ground breathes, gravity is light or crushing, colours invert, figures move only while unwatched, time hitches, your size changes, the dream repeats itself.

There is no end to it. The ground loops in every direction and stacks upward as long as anyone climbs.

Every minute inside rolls a chance of knowledge, reported when you wake.

worldAdventures.title: Adventures on the Map
worldAdventures.description:
Some world map squares carry a "???" marker, redrawn once a day. Stand on it and Investigate plays a branching adventure written for that place.

The last node pays out: a relic, gear, salvage, money, a fight with something native, a minigame, an augment, a change of faction standing, a crime filed against you, a rest, or nothing.

The leader goes in and the companion at their shoulder comments in their own register. Some choices are only offered to a leader of a particular temperament, and the prose is combinatorial.

A biome carries one marker, two if it is very large, and a named place carries its own on top. An answered square stays answered.

worldBologna.title: Bologna
worldBologna.description:
Bologna is in the game as itself, rasterised from OpenStreetMap into a grid of large cells that join seamlessly at the borders.

Every rasterised building has a door on its south face and every door is a way in. Most are homes; a share are shops and inns, seeded per cell and per tile, so a door is always the same business.

The cells carry no hand placed events. The city is populated at runtime: townspeople drawn from the world's own faces and from Bolognesi born there, plus wildlife by habitat, street animals on pavements, waterfowl and fish in the canals, birds on rooftops.

worldPlatformer.title: Platformer Maps
worldPlatformer.description:
On a map tagged as a platform stage the controls become a side scroller: left and right walk, space jumps, shift runs, gravity pulls, and jumping against a wall kicks off it.

Ladders are climbed with up. Companions follow your exact path a moment behind.

worldFlying.title: Flying
worldFlying.description:
Flight moves you like an airship: freely, in any direction, over everything. Confirm lands you.

It comes from particular items, skills and vehicles rather than being held permanently.

worldConnections.title: The Map of Maps
worldConnections.description:
A second map shows every map you know and how they connect, built from the transfer events and doors between them.

Click a node to set it as destination and the shortest path lights up. A compass appears in the corner pointing at the next waypoint and goes away on arrival.

worldTreasure.title: Chests and Treasure Rooms
worldTreasure.description:
Chest contents are generated against the party's median level. An emptied chest stays empty, and open chests stay open.

Some maps hide treasure rooms: reachable, randomly placed rooms with heavier contents.

worldTechTree.title: Research and Discovery
worldTechTree.description:
Seven trees of discovery, one per discipline: Social Sciences, Alchemistry, Technomagica, Physics, Arcane, Mathematics, Astronomy, Theotecnical.

The scientific trees follow real progress from 2001 to 2012. Arcane and Technomagica follow the rediscovery of lost magic and its fusion with machinery. Theotecnical follows the Vatican rebuilding its dogma around engines. Each also carries fringe branches and a few nodes generated from the world seed.

Completed nodes record the leader who got there first. Researching one consumes crafting materials and returns most of that cost as refined byproducts.

travelOverview.title: Fast Travel
travelOverview.description:
Any place marked as a destination can be travelled to instead of walked to. Bus stops and signposts open the travel screen.

A destination and a mode put you on a travel map for that transport, with a countdown that keeps running while you open menus or fight and survives scene changes. At zero you arrive.

Companions talk in transit, vehicle crews sleep in shifts, and the world clock keeps moving.

travelModes.title: The Thirty Ways to Travel
travelModes.description:
Each destination lists the transports that reach it. There are thirty, trading money against time.

Walking is free and slowest. A bicycle is cheap and slightly quicker, a horse better than a bicycle, and car sharing or the camper cost fuel instead of money.

Bus, train, taxi, boat and ferry are the ordinary fares. The train is fast for its price, the taxi the same speed for twice as much.

Flights, limousines, helicopters and private jets are expensive, a private jet running ten times walking speed. Cruises, submarines, balloons and zeppelins are slow and dear.

The exotic tier holds magic carpets and dragons, teleport circles at twenty times walking speed for a modest fee, hypermetro, maglev and hyperloop, and then starships, wormholes, quantum jumps, time machines and dimensional crossings. A dimensional crossing costs a thousand times the base fare and is a thousand times as fast.

Cost is the base fare times distance, and speed divides the time.

vehiclesOverview.title: Owning a Vehicle
vehiclesOverview.description:
A vehicle is proven by an item. Holding the key, the deed or the broom puts it in the Vehicles menu and makes it summonable and drivable.

Vehicles are parked in the world, not carried, and each one's position is stored, world square and underground layer included. Where several sit on one tile, interacting asks which you meant.

Walking up to a parked vehicle opens its menu: drive, enter the interior, use storage, refuel, repair.

The camper, the car and the starship have walk in interiors with storage holds.

vehicleCamper.title: Vehicle: The Camper
vehicleCamper.description:
The largest vehicle. A hundred litres of fuel, a walk in interior with beds and storage, repairable and upgradable, refuels at any roadside pump.

A ground vehicle, so it crosses road tiles faster than open country, and fast travel by camper costs fuel rather than money.

Two workshop modules extend it. Aquatic makes it float and dive, with C to dive and surface. Flight fits rotors, with F to take off and land.

Driving it opens a 3D scene, and a crew lives aboard it.

vehicleCar.title: Vehicle: The Car
vehicleCar.description:
Faster than the camper and much smaller. Sixty litres of fuel, a small interior, refuels at any pump, takes the road bonus, and fast travel by car costs fuel rather than money.

Any parked car on the map can be stolen: face it, press the action button and choose to steal. That opens the lockpicking minigame and needs a lockpick, or a skeleton key, which opens it outright. Success hands you its keys and removes the car from the world. Failure files a vehicle theft against you.

vehicleBike.title: Vehicle: The Bike
vehicleBike.description:
Human powered, so it needs no fuel and cannot run dry. The fastest vehicle available early, takes the road bonus, and has no interior, no storage and no repair costs.

No crew rota: the rider does everything.

vehicleBroom.title: Vehicle: The Flying Broom
vehicleBroom.description:
Needs no fuel, works indoors, and stows into your pack as an item.

It flies, so it passes over every tile of every map: walls, water, cliffs and events. It lands on anything that can be stood on, rooftops and bridges included, and is boarded from the tile it landed on.

It takes no road bonus.

vehicleBoat.title: Vehicle: The Boat
vehicleBoat.description:
An inflatable dinghy. No fuel, no interior, no storage, no repairs, and it travels only on open water.

The party is drawn aboard: everyone on the benches, bow first, facing the way they are going, with the pet in the stern.

vehicleStarship.title: Vehicle: The Starship
vehicleStarship.description:
Two hundred litres of fuel and a full walk in interior. It cannot be refuelled at a roadside pump.

Hull, layout and appearance are generated from a set of trait axes and can be edited.

It needs no driver and flies itself, so its crew page covers living aboard rather than driving. It is used from the star map.

vehicleFuel.title: Fuel
vehicleFuel.description:
The camper, the car and the starship burn fuel. The bike, the broom and the boat do not.

Fuel is bought at pumps at a price that moves with the world's oil market. The camper and the car fill at any roadside pump; the starship cannot.

Consumption is by distance and differs per vehicle, with a gauge in the corner while driving. Running dry strands you.

vehicleRepair.title: Vehicle Damage and Repair
vehicleRepair.description:
A vehicle has twelve parts, each with its own health. Engine, transmission, brakes and steering are critical and stop it dead when broken; battery, alternator, radiator, fuel system, exhaust, suspension, tyres and body only cost performance.

Damage comes from what you hit. Something soft marks the front only; another vehicle at road speed is felt throughout. The notification names the parts.

Repairs consume crafting materials, scaled by the depth of the repair. While riding, the vehicle's condition is drawn as an HP bar on the party HUD.

vehicleUpgrades.title: The Workshop
vehicleUpgrades.description:
Vehicles are upgraded with crafting materials at the workshop.

Four upgrades, three levels each: acceleration, speed, fuel capacity and structural health. Two one off modules, camper only: aquatic, which floats and dives, and flight, which fits rotors.

Aerodynamic work reduces how much game time a world map tile costs.

Each level costs more exotic materials, from steel and plastic through titanium and circuitry to varlenian matter, nanotubes and quantum components.

vehicleCrew.title: The Crew
vehicleCrew.description:
The leader takes the wheel when a journey starts, and only the driver earns the vehicle's specialization experience.

Time at the wheel is tracked per person as strain, and alertness is the party's sleep meter less that member's strain. Below 40% the wheel passes to the best rested member above that line, and everyone not driving sheds strain. When nobody is fit to relieve the driver, they keep going and you are told.

Passengers sleep. Naps start below 40% sleep and run to full or to the end of the journey. They wake when the nap ends, when the party gets out, when someone enters the cabin, and on a crash, which also keeps them awake for the next hour.

The bike and the broom have no rota. The starship has no driver, and its crew tends one need at a time out of the hold.

vehicleDriving.title: Driving in 3D
vehicleDriving.description:
Driving the camper opens a 3D road scene built from the world map: the same grid of biomes, mountains as noise height fields, water flat and blue, roads as dual lane asphalt, everything else ground in that biome's colour. Coastlines slope into the sea, and cities, forests and cacti are scattered along the way.

Three views, swapped with Tab or Y: first person behind an animated wheel and a working dash, chase camera with zoom, and a free roam cabin view entered through a door.

W throttles, Shift is turbo, S brakes and reverses, A and D steer, space is the handbrake, the mouse looks.

The model has a five speed automatic with an RPM engine note, lateral slip so the handbrake drifts, grip that differs between asphalt, dirt, grass, sand, snow and rock, gravity on slopes, and a chassis that follows the terrain.

Traffic runs nine models, hatchback to city bus, built at true size against the camper. They brake, take junctions and can be crashed into, and a bus shoves harder than a hatchback.

On foot the leader's weapon is in hand, and the d-pad steps through every weapon in the bags they can hold. Enemies matched to the biome idle by the roadside.

roadTraffic.title: Traffic, Roadkill and Theft
roadTraffic.description:
Map traffic is driven by the game rather than by event pages.

A car occupies as many tiles as its sprite is long, for every purpose: it never clips a wall it passes, cars collide bodywork against bodywork, and anyone under the bodywork is run over. Only a moving car hits anything, town traffic brakes for people and highway traffic does not.

Being hit knocks you clear and triggers an accident. An NPC hit by a car takes injury conditions written onto their profile; a creature hit hard enough dies and leaves a corpse.

Driving over someone yourself injures them, drops their opinion of every party member, and files a hit and run. Ramming a creature flings it off the bonnet the first two times; from the third the odds it turns and fights climb steeply.

Occasionally a car pulls over and its driver gets out, walks about and later drives on. That driver is an ordinary wandering NPC, and the car sits parked and stealable meanwhile.

peopleOverview.title: People Are Real Here
peopleOverview.description:
Every person on the map carries a full profile, generated from their name and the world seed:

- a personality out of twenty five archetypes, which sets how they speak
- traits, the same ones your characters carry
- an ideology on five axes: economy, authority, tradition, militarism, mysticism
- wealth, skills, inventory and equipment
- a faction, a home, a job and a schedule
- a backstory drawn from your world's history
- a medical history, past diseases and badly healed bones included

Part of the population is animals, minted from the same system. A creature on a beast class is non sentient: no conversation, no politics, no savings, no property.

peopleEmpathize.title: The Empathize Panel
peopleEmpathize.description:
Talking to someone properly opens the Empathize panel: identity, history, biology, health, romantic life, daily life, politics, and a log of their last conversations.

From it you can talk, praise, insult, joke, give, trade, court, propose, recruit, and read why they feel as they do about you.

Standings are per party member, and only the member doing the talking moves theirs.

A free chat field takes typed input and generates a reply. With the local language model enabled it writes the reply; otherwise a Markov chain does.

peopleOpinion.title: How Somebody Decides What They Think of You
peopleOpinion.description:
An NPC's opinion of one of your characters is built from four parts:

- base opinion, moved by everything you have done to them
- trait compatibility, applied before a word is spoken
- ideology, how close your creeds sit on the five axes, worth up to a dozen points either way
- hygiene, how the two of you smell to each other right now

Gaining standing also feeds the social need of whoever gained it.

Attraction is tracked apart from opinion. Conversation, gifts and trade move opinion only; courting moves attraction, and a romantic move reads trait compatibility and hygiene a second time at a heavier weight.

peopleLives.title: People Have Lives
peopleLives.description:
Everyone's life advances whenever time does: minute by minute, and through any skip.

- they are born somewhere on a date and keep a record of every move since, with reasons
- they meet, date, marry, divorce and separate, preferring partners from their own settlement
- they hold careers from the real job list, with a history from their first working year, changes as they age, and retirement
- dishonest ones carry convictions, sentences served off screen and outstanding bounties, and a conviction can cost someone their job

A year spent in cryogenic sleep is a year in which everyone aged, changed jobs, married and buried each other.

peopleTalking.title: What People Say to Each Other
peopleTalking.description:
Two people who wander close together stop, face each other and hold a conversation, one line at a time in thought bubbles. The tone, positive, negative, neutral or a debate, comes from what they think of each other and from their personalities. Finishing one moves both opinions.

People sharing a room while busy trade two line exchanges without stopping.

Each of the twenty five personalities has its own lines for weather and time of day, its own inner monologue, and its own openers and closers.

The last twenty conversations of every person can be read in their panel.

peopleSettlements.title: Settlements and What Happens To Them
peopleSettlements.description:
Every settlement carries three civic meters. Prosperity comes from employment, the national economy and recent events; security from crime per head, the honesty of the local captain of the guard, national stability and how wanted you are; mood from the other two plus unrest, festivals, epidemics and street traffic.

Episodes sit on top of them:

- crime wave: starts when security collapses. Crime pays better and the crackdown catches more thieves, so the wave breaks itself
- boom and bust: start at the extremes of prosperity and swing hiring, crime, divorce, shop prices and market sentiment, then erode their own cause
- festival: declared by a thriving town. Mood and bustle up, shops fuller, pickpockets working the crowds
- epidemic: rare, and worse in miserable towns. Mood, hiring and shop traffic collapse until it burns out

Unemployment feeds crime, crime feeds crackdowns, crackdowns feed prisons, prisons feed unemployment. All of it reaches the news, the stock market, hiring and gossip.

peoplePolitics.title: Politics
peoplePolitics.description:
Every hyperpower has a government, and their shapes differ: theocracies, single party states, parliamentary monarchies, technocracies, sultanates, divine pantheons, serene republics, corporatocracies, warband confederacies. Each has parties, orders or clans, a political class with charisma, integrity, cunning and ambition, a head of state, and meters for legitimacy, stability, unrest, economy and treasury.

Elections run in each power's own idiom: general elections, papal conclaves over several ballots, politburo plenums announcing 99% results, wealth weighted shareholder meetings, goblin moots where the runner up risks being eaten, divine ascension tournaments, palace successions, and the Archive's Great Examination.

Between elections: scandals, edicts, protests, riots, coups, revolutions, assassinations, referendums, and rulers ageing and dying.

Every person has a political identity: five axis ideology, a party, an engagement level from apathetic to organizer, a voting record, and grudges against the parties that beat theirs.

Each settlement elects a mayor every year, who appoints a captain of the guard, a tax collector and a high priest from among their allies.

peopleFactions.title: Factions and Reputation
peopleFactions.description:
Eighteen factions. Standing with each runs from -100 to +100, moved by contracts taken, crimes committed, adventures resolved and sides taken.

Factions answer to hyperpowers. A faction with a hyperpower is a branch of it, so credit earned with a parent can carry its branches.

Standing decides what work is offered, what prices are quoted, who will speak to you, and which seats you may take.

peopleONU.title: The Assembly
peopleONU.description:
Every hyperpower holds a seat on neutral ground inside the Omega Tower. Once a game week the delegations argue about alliances, trade, war and recent events.

A party member can take a seat. The seat, the standing it earns and the weekly stipend are that character's alone, and the stipend scales with their standing with the power they serve. Let it fall far enough and they are dismissed. Only powers that already think neutrally or well of them will take them, a character joins once, and resigning costs far more than joining paid.

A session rolls one to three motions. Two to five delegations take the floor, each in its own voice, you answer, and every seat votes. Ballots are public, turning each named tile green or red as it is read, or secret, shuffled unlabelled so only the tally is certain.

Grave motions, war, admission, territory, artifacts, theonuclear devices and the goblin question, go to the Security Council: the five strongest powers left standing by your century. Majority carries and the Secretary General breaks a tie; without one, the motion fails.

The Tourists hold a chair with no ballot, take the floor when they like, and admit nobody.

lawCrime.title: Crime and Bounty
lawCrime.description:
Every crime is filed by name with its own bounty value, and your bounty is the sum of them. Deliberate crimes: theft, breaking and entering, vehicle theft. Accidental ones too, such as running someone over.

Bounty lowers the security meter of settlements you are in, becomes gossip, changes how the guard behaves, and is read out in court.

The record can be viewed at any time and settled through the police portal.

lawPolice.title: The Police Portal
lawPolice.description:
The N€police application on the Hypernet is the continental police portal, and it settles your record without waiting for you to be caught.

- case file: every charge with its fine, settled one at a time or all at once
- self-report: confess something not yet registered, at half the usual fine
- custody: turn yourself in, or request a hearing before Eris

Both custody options leave the computer, because the cells and the courtroom are places on the map.

lawTrial.title: The Trial
lawTrial.description:
Justice is administered by Eris, and a trial is generated rather than scripted. The courtroom, gallery, staff and ambience are rolled fresh each time, and she cites invented case law and produces invented exhibits mid hearing.

Counsel is retained before the hearing opens: hire one of five advocates, nominate a party member, or stand alone. The five are people from your world, fixed for its lifetime, and recruiting one strikes them off the bar.

The brief shows each option's level, INT, WIS, Law level, opinion of you, fee, and the projected odds of every outcome, computed with the model the verdict runs on. The odds swing on Eris's mood, and in some moods she throws counsel out, which loses their bonus and does not refund the fee.

Representing yourself, or having a companion stand up, earns a few points of the Law specialization per hearing, which feeds back into the odds. A professional teaches the party nothing.

The hearing is a plea, then a series of choices, then a verdict that depends heavily on her mood. Evenings spent with Eris raise a bond, and a defendant she has dined with meets a warmer mood wheel, a lower conviction chance and shorter sentences.

Sandbox mode has a reverse trial, where you play Eris.

lawPrison.title: Sentences and Prison
lawPrison.description:
Sentences come in two shapes. A named term is served by the game clock: time passes in the cells and the bounty is cleared on release. An open ended sentence has no release date and grinds the bounty down day by day.

Turning yourself in at the police portal goes straight to the second kind without a hearing.

On release, Eris comments, according to how the two of you stand.

lawEris.title: Dating Eris
lawEris.description:
Eris can be courted, and an evening with her is a generated scene.

It happens in a biome, and each biome owns its opening, its questions, its romantic beat, its chaotic beat, its shared activity and its local incidents. A scenario is rolled on top, picnic, seance, stakeout and others, so one biome hosts many evenings.

Her mood is rolled from sixteen: playful, romantic, chaotic, nervous, confident, caring, guilty, crazed, psyched out, high on solipsism, eldritch, melancholy, smug, paranoid, prophetic, bored. It can shift mid date. In the eldritch mood her lines warp, her pulse reads things that are not numbers, and the portrait misbehaves.

Each date also rolls a register, sincere, capricious or completely bonkers, which scales how often the evening is interrupted and how hard her feelings swing. She interrupts with dares, up to robbing a bank. Your own answers are generated too, and how she takes one is a roll of her mood.

Two heartbeats are drawn on screen, yours and hers. She remembers past dates, keeps a separate score for every party member, and sometimes turns towards one of your companions mid date.

The first date that ends well pays a blade seed, once per save.

societyMail.title: The Post
societyMail.description:
A party can write to another party in the same world, or to a party in a different world on your machine. The letter waits in their mailbox until someone plays them.

A letter carries a delivery date on the recipient world's clock, and the sender can hold it back by days, months or years. Writing to your own party with a delay is a letter to your future self.

Money and goods can be enclosed. They leave the sender's pockets at once and are handed over when the recipient collects them.

Post inside one world is free. Crossing to another is priced on the two commodities that survive the crossing, oil and souls: their prices multiplied, doubled once per step of dimensional distance, never less than three hundred thousand euros.

societyNews.title: The News
societyNews.description:
The world writes its own news, and items carry effects: property prices, shop occupancy, market sentiment.

Settlement episodes, riots, coups, elections, epidemics and the mayor's divorce all become headlines. The real estate market moves on them, the stock market takes sentiment from them, and people talk about them.

societyDiary.title: The Party Diary
societyDiary.description:
The diary is the record one party keeps of its own life, written as it happens.

It takes in journeys and arrivals, landings and warps, first entry into a named place, dungeon floors, sleeping and waiting, cryogenic sleep, fights won and lost, bosses, arena streaks, people joining and leaving, deaths, levels, pets, creatures talked round, births, friendships, enmities, courtships, evenings with Eris, diseases, limbs lost, augments, surgery, notable finds, purchases and sales, thefts, property, loans, share trades, crimes, trials, prison, shifts worked, crops, forging, cooking, brewing, building, skills, research, quests, bestiary entries, minigames, television and dreams.

Not recorded: ordinary conversation, statue descriptions, states coming and going, discarded items.

Entries are stored as keys, so a diary written in one language reads correctly in another. The banter system takes the newest lines and turns them into what the party talks about.

societyTopics.title: Conversation Topics
societyTopics.description:
Some dialogue teaches a topic, written in square brackets in the line where it appears. Once one character hears it, the whole party knows it.

A dialogue option that requires a topic is invisible until then, not greyed out.

Every topic learned is announced. The Topics tab of this book lists them with who knows each one, and some have a page of their own.

societyArmy.title: Armies
societyArmy.description:
Beyond the party of three there is an army. Troops are recruited by faction, up to a hundred, and the count is drawn over your sprite on the world map.
